results.question: What do the screen-combat and fight-choreography books say about making a punch read as re
results.answer:
The books treat a believable punch as a shared illusion: the fist itself stops short of real impact (“staged near-contact”), and what sells it is the receiver’s recoil plus the camera’s reaction, locked to the exact instant the hit lands [S1][S3]. It is explicitly an illusion — “a theatrical combative art form” that fabricates a physical confrontation rather than transplanting a real technique onto film [S4].

## The four levers

| Lever | What the books say |
|---|---|
| **Camera angle** | Framing distance and angle are artistic choices about how subjects fill the screen, but they must still convey the information the scene needs [S2]. Effective angles let the audience “comprehend and believe” the move, and brawls often read best framed extremely close [S8][S14]. A cut mid-move also demands a shift in angle or framing, or the edit feels jarring [S6]. |
| **Distance to the strike** | Real punching travels through the target — board breakers punch “a spot a few inches past,” not the surface. Movie hits invert that: the punch is pulled and stops essentially on contact, so a stunt stomach punch lands on the fatty layer under the skin with no follow-through [S13]. Guarding against clipping and ending in a deliberate release keeps that near-contact honest [S5][S3]. |
| **The reaction** | Half of the effect is the receiving body’s recoil and recovery, set up by the strike’s staging and screen direction [S3]. The camera joins in: a right haymaker traveling screen-left-to-right earns a little screen-right flinch at impact — the camera “feels the punch,” and the whole world “gets knocked slightly sideways.” That shudder also covers up small alignment slips between the two actors [S1]. |
| **Timing** | The response locks to contact rather than preceding or lagging it: the camera flinches “just as the hit lands” [S1], and the exchange runs on two-character timing — step-in and strike, block or dodge, staged contact, recoil and recovery [S3]. Editing is the third clock: cuts should heighten the fight’s rhythm with logical continuity, and a cut on a move requires the next angle as its payoff [S6][S14]. |

Underneath all four levers sit story choices: believable cause and motivation, a fighter’s skill set matching the character, and martial acting that sells the moment [S7][S14].

## Laban effort: the vocabulary of the hit

The Laban workbook supplies the movement language these effects use: the Effort dimension has two poles per factor — Weight (strong↔light), Time (quick/sudden↔sustained), Space (direct↔indirect), and Flow (bound↔free) — with Body covering weight shift and sequencing [S11]. The workbook defines these for movement in general, so applying them to a punch is an extrapolation, but the mapping is clean: strong Weight reads as force, sudden Time snaps the strike and speeds the reaction, direct Space gives the punch its target line, and bound Flow describes the “pulled” control of a stunt punch — the fist stops because the actor holds it back, not because the target stops it [S11][S13]. The receiver’s recoil is the same grammar in reverse: sudden and strong, then resolving into free Flow as the body recovers.

One caveat: the books give principles, not measurements — no lenses, standoff distances in feet, or exact frame counts for the reaction lag. The implied rule is that the response is simultaneous with impact, because visible delay would break the near-contact illusion [S1][S3].
